simple|en|What is high availability?.explanation: High availability means keeping a service running with very little downtime, even when something fails. In Azure this is done by removing single points of failure: you spread workloads across multiple machines, zones, or regions, and add health checks so a broken piece is skipped automatically. The goal is not 'never goes down'. It is 'stays up almost all the time and recovers fast'.

keyTerms.meaning: Service Level Agreement: the % uptime a provider promises, e.g. 99.9%.
Having spare copies of a component so one failure does not stop the service.
Automatically switching to a healthy copy when the primary one fails.

simple|en|Explain scalability vs elastic.explanation: Scalability is the ability to handle more or less load by adding resources. Elasticity is a special kind of scalability: it adds resources automatically when demand rises and removes them when it falls, so you only pay for what you need right now. Scalable means 'can grow'. Elastic means 'grows and shrinks on its own'.

keyTerms.meaning: A bigger machine (more CPU/RAM). Also called vertical scaling.
More machines side by side. Also called horizontal scaling.
Rules that add or remove instances based on metrics like CPU.

simple|en|IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS?.explanation: These are three layers of cloud service. IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) gives you raw machines and networking, and you install and look after the operating system and apps. PaaS (Platform as a Service) gives you a ready runtime, so you only bring your code and data while the provider runs the OS and servers. SaaS (Software as a Service) is a finished app you just use, like webmail. The more the provider handles, the less you manage.

keyTerms.meaning: You manage the OS and apps; the provider manages hardware and network. e.g. Azure Virtual Machines.
You manage apps and data only; the provider manages the OS and servers. e.g. Azure App Service.
The provider manages everything; you just use the app. e.g. Microsoft 365.

SaaS is a fully running tuck shop: you walk in and buy a cool drink, and someone else runs the whole thing.

simple|en|What is an availability zone?.explanation: An availability zone is a separate physical location inside one Azure region, with its own power, cooling, and network. Zones are far enough apart that a flood or fire in one is unlikely to hit another, but close enough for fast replication. Putting your workload across two or three zones protects you from a single datacenter failure while staying in the same region.

keyTerms.meaning: A geographic area with one or more datacenters, e.g. South Africa North.
An independent datacenter location within a region, with its own power, cooling, and network.
A service that automatically spreads across multiple zones.

simple|en|What does the shared responsib.explanation: The shared responsibility model says the cloud provider and the customer each own different layers of security and management. The provider always owns the physical datacenter, network, and host hardware. What you own depends on the service model: with IaaS you own the OS and everything above it, with PaaS you own your app and data, and with SaaS you mostly own your data and who can access it. Your data and access are always your responsibility.

keyTerms.meaning: The datacenter, network, physical hosts, and (for PaaS and SaaS) the OS.
Your data, access, and identities, and (for IaaS) the OS and patches.
Your data and who can reach it. This never moves to the provider.

But you lock your own door, decide who gets a key, and keep your valuables safe (your data and access). Even in a hotel (SaaS), you still lock your room and guard your suitcase.
